tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — WOODLAND PERENNIAL BROME
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1252) — Follow several stems down to the base and look for a small perennial clump. The Flora describes drooping spikelets.

Hairy woodland brome is a native perennial of mesic wooded sites, with culms commonly 65–120(150) cm, relatively soft blades 6–19 mm wide, and open 10–25 cm panicles. A rooted persistent crown is important because native Texas brome and introduced Japanese/lanceolate bromes are annuals. EPA and Copenhagen photos plus new true in-ground Austin woodland-habit panel 8 show different stages and live leafy bunching, but NOT an extracted connected perennial crown or perennial age proof.
tiles.short: Follow a loose, often drooping panicle to a persistent, non-rhizomatous perennial bunch; confirm on mature spikelets, not droop alone.
tiles.status: THREE SAME-SPECIES HABIT VIEWS (TEXAS WOODLAND INCLUDED) — EXPOSED PERENNIAL ROOTS STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR — MEMBRANOUS LIGULE
tiles.details: Open a fresh leaf at the inner collar and measure the short 0.5–2 mm glabrous membranous ligule with a 1-mm ruler. It is not the often retrorse hairs on the CLOSED sheath or hairy nodes. Leaf blades are usually 6–19 mm wide; sheaths may be conspicuously hairy but can vary. Do not use sheath pubescence alone to determine species. Actual newly archived panels 7 (blade/sheath exterior) and 9 (true culm joint) show the correct STRUCTURES to examine, but neither opens the short INNER ligule at a calibrated 1-mm scale. It remains a photographic hold, not an arrow target.
tiles.short: Look inside the blade–sheath junction for a 0.5–2 mm erose membrane; no auricles.
tiles.status: REAL EXTERIOR SHEATH AND NODE PHOTOGRAPHED — TRUE INNER LIGULE/MM SCALE NOT CERTIFIED

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE A RIPE MULTIFLORED SPIKELET
tiles.details: Choose 2–3 ripe, source-authenticated spikelets still attached to the branched panicle, measure their complete length and count florets under 10–20×. Published ranges include (13)15–30 mm and (4)5–10(13) florets. The two basal persistent bracts are GLUMES; the overlapping bracts around individual florets are LEMMAS. New exact-species source photos 10 and 11 show fresh and dry real Texas spikelets. The comparison photos in panels 1–5 show DIFFERENT Bromus species; never use them as proof of pubescens reproductive dimensions or assert these fresh photos have measured floret counts.
tiles.short: Usually 15–30 mm (occasionally ~13 mm) with about 5–10 florets; outer pair are glumes.
tiles.status: FRESH AND DRY REAL TEXAS MULTIFLORED SPIKELETS PHOTOGRAPHED; ACTUAL SCALE/FLORET COUNTS PENDING

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUME VEINS — IMPORTANT NATIVE/INTRODUCED SPLIT
tiles.details: Dissect the basal glume pair from a ripe B. pubescens spikelet. Under transmitted light count the lower glume's usual 1 vein and upper glume's usual 3 (sometimes 5) veins; both are normally awnless. Japanese brome often has substantially more glume veins, but native Texas brome ALSO has the 1/3 pattern. Therefore 1/3 glumes do NOT by themselves prove woodland brome: compare rooted life history and mature lemmas. The additional exact-species fresh and dry green/bract views (panels 10/11) are not backlit or separated into individual glumes; no exact-species photo supports a vein-count arrow.
tiles.short: Lower glume 4–8 mm, usually ONE vein; upper 5–10 mm, usually THREE (rarely five).

tiles.heading: 05 · HAIRY LEMMA, PALEA AND STRAIGHT AWN
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1252) — Turn a lemma under a hand lens. The Flora describes its surface as usually densely hairy.

Remove one mature floret and distinguish the 8–12 mm LEMMA from the usually shorter PALEA, whose keels may be ciliate. The lemma commonly has fine hairs on the back and margins but can be sparse or nearly glabrous; never reject pubescens solely because one floret looks smooth. Measure its single straight ~3–8 mm awn emerging near/below the apex (usually within ~1.5 mm). Descriptions of tiny lemma-tip teeth differ; do not fabricate a bifid apex. A new dry actual species spikelet macro in panel 11 better shows real overlapping elongated bracts and awns, but it still cannot certify separate dorsal hair insertion, palea keels or awn origin from these pixels.
tiles.short: Mature lemma 8–12 mm, often hairy across back and margins; straight awn usually 3–8 mm.

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLIC-READY GATE
tiles.details: B. texensis (panel 2) is a native annual with often 1/3-veined glumes, so protect it from misidentification; B. japonicus (panel 1) is an introduced annual, commonly with higher glume vein counts; B. lanceolatus (panel 3) is introduced with long ~25–50 mm many-flowered spikelets; B. catharticus (panels 4–5) is comparison-only and has broader flattened, short/no-awn spikelets. These are look-alike photos, not pubescens anatomy evidence. NEW five Texas source-labelled real woodland photos at panels 7–11 now show an actual in-ground bunch, external sheath and stem node, living green and dry spikelets; none exposes an intact 0.5–2-mm true ligule, connected extracted perennial root system, backlit glumes or separated hairy lemma. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same-plant rooted crown/panicle, true measured ligule, backlit glume pair and hairy mature lemma with scale. NEEDS_SITE_QA: exact rights, provenance, annotations, comparison labels and mobile gallery. Retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until evidence and live QA are verified.
tiles.short: Texas brome shares 1/3-veined glumes but is annual; Japanese brome has more glume veins; rescuegrass has broad flat spikelets.
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 7 REAL SPECIES PHOTOS / 12 PANELS; ROOT/LIGULE/GLUMES/LEMMA AND PAGES QA OPEN

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: NATIVE WOODLAND BROME: follow an intact rooted plant to a PERSISTENT, non-rhizomatous perennial tuft, broad soft blades and an open drooping panicle. Under 10–20× inspect a 13–30 mm multi-flowered spikelet: lower glume normally ONE-veined (4–8 mm), upper THREE-veined (occasionally 5; 5–10 mm), and 8–12 mm lemmas usually hairy over the BACK (occasionally sparse or glabrous), each with a straight 3–8 mm awn. The 0.5–2 mm true membranous ligule has a jagged edge and no auricles. Introduced Japanese brome typically has more glume veins; native Texas brome also has a 1/3-veined pair but is ANNUAL. No existing target photo proves the glume veins, lemma hairs or ligule: keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with both archived exact-species photographs; trace the branching panicle to a single multi-flowered spikelet, then locate the rooted basal crown where actually visible. Never conclude a rhizomatous perennial merely from one photographic frame.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Open a fresh leaf at the inner collar and measure the short 0.5–2 mm glabrous membranous ligule with a 1-mm ruler. It is not the often retrorse hairs on the CLOSED sheath or hairy nodes. Leaf blades are usually 6–19 mm wide; sheaths may be conspicuously hairy but can vary. Do not use sheath pubescence alone to determine species. Actual newly archived panels 7 (blade/sheath exterior) and 9 (true culm joint) show the correct STRUCTURES to examine, but neither opens the short INNER ligule at a calibrated 1-mm scale. It remains a photographic hold, not an arrow target.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Choose 2–3 ripe, source-authenticated spikelets still attached to the branched panicle, measure their complete length and count florets under 10–20×. Published ranges include (13)15–30 mm and (4)5–10(13) florets. The two basal persistent bracts are GLUMES; the overlapping bracts around individual florets are LEMMAS. New exact-species source photos 10 and 11 show fresh and dry real Texas spikelets. The comparison photos in panels 1–5 show DIFFERENT Bromus species; never use them as proof of pubescens reproductive dimensions or assert these fresh photos have measured floret counts.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: NATIVE WOODLAND BROME: follow an intact rooted plant to a PERSISTENT, non-rhizomatous perennial tuft, broad soft blades and an open drooping panicle. No existing target photo proves the glume veins, lemma hairs or ligule: keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
memory_rule: JAPANESE: annual, flexuous awned head, higher glume veins. TEXAS: annual, lower ONE & upper THREE glume veins. LANCEOLATE: giant many-flowered spikelets. WOODLAND: perennial + hairy lemmas. RESCUE: broad flat short/no-awn units (comparison only).
safety_note: Both local gallery images verified in metadata, but neither proves a measured lemma, ligule or glume anatomy. Hairiness is variable and glumes may themselves be pubescent; do not teach glumes as invariably glabrous. Measurements are literature ranges, not verified from the two site images. No new photograph or arrow added.
field_rule: WOODED PERENNIAL BROME: confirm durable crown and true hairs on mature lemmas; match a measured spikelet and sheath/collar photo before separating native pubescens from annual bromes.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
